chen-clan-frieze.title: The Plaster Frieze of Chen Clan Hall
chen-clan-frieze.subtitle: Chen Clan Hall · An Apprentice's Summer
chen-clan-frieze.quote: Plaster ages; craft has no fear of age.
chen-clan-frieze.intro: You are the apprentice of a lime-plaster master. The roof ridge of Chen Clan Hall needs mending, your master has fallen ill at the last minute, and all that is left is you and half a bucket of plaster.

chen-1.title: The Gap in the Roof Ridge
chen-1.text: A crack has opened along the tile ridge of Chen Clan Hall, and rainwater is seeping into the plaster. Your master says between coughs: 'Go up there and do as I taught you.' You shoulder the bucket of plaster, and your legs turn weak.

chen-2a.title: The First Stroke
chen-2a.text: You climb onto the ridge, where the wind is strong enough to make you unsteady on your feet. The moment your trowel comes down, the old plaster crumbles and a copper wire shows through. Your master said the copper wire is the skeleton—it must not be pulled out.

chen-2b.title: Your Uncle-Master's Terms
chen-2b.text: Your uncle-master is willing to help, but on one condition: you sign a paper saying that once the repair is done, the credit belongs to him. You hold the pen, your hand frozen in mid-air.

chen-3.title: The Rain Comes
chen-3.text: Halfway through, it starts to rain. Wet plaster fears water more than anything—one wash and it falls apart. You look at the roof ridge, then at the visitors below who cannot get out of the rain in time.

chen-4a.title: Colour After the Rain
chen-4a.text: When the rain stops, a white bloom has risen on the surface of the plaster. Your master said that at a time like this you must lay on a thin coat, and only then will the colour come out even. Your hand slips, and you put it on too thick.

chen-4b.title: Cracks Made in Haste
chen-4b.text: You rush the work in the rain and paint before the plaster dries. The next day the colour has cracked into flakes, like fish scales. Visitors look up and point at the ridge, laughing.

chen-5.title: The Master Comes to Look
chen-5.text: Before the day is over, your master returns from the hospital. He does not scold you; he only brushes his fingers lightly over the plaster and asks: 'Where do you think it still is not good enough?'

chen-e1.title: Ending · A Name on the Roof Ridge
chen-e1.text: Your master nods: 'With the skeleton in place, the plaster can stand firm.' Years later, you repair another roof ridge at Chen Clan Hall on your own. When it comes time to sign, you write down your master's name first, then your own.
chen-e1.endingText: Plaster ages; craft has no fear of age.

chen-e2.title: Ending · One More Thin Coat
chen-e2.text: Your master smiles: 'Only those who admit it is not enough can truly learn.' You scrape away the thick layer overnight and lay it thin again. By dawn, the colour on the ridge is as even as a piece of old jade.
chen-e2.endingText: Slow work does not always mean fine work, but being willing to change is always better than not.

chen-1: Do as the master said—go up alone
Go and find your uncle-master for help
chen-2a: Keep the copper wire and patch it slowly
Pull out the rotten wire and redo it
chen-2b: Sign it—fix the roof first, talk later
Do not sign—take it on yourself
chen-3: Cover it with a rain sheet and wait for the rain to stop
Work through the rain to save time
chen-4a: Leave it—you cannot tell from far away
chen-4b: Admit the mistake openly and redo it
While no one is looking, touch up the colour
chen-5: Tell your master the copper wire was saved
Tell your master the colour is not even enough

guangxiao-bodhi.title: The Bodhi Tree of Guangxiao Temple
guangxiao-bodhi.subtitle: Guangxiao Temple · A Thousand Years of One Tree
guangxiao-bodhi.quote: The tree has not gone anywhere; it is people who come and go.
guangxiao-bodhi.intro: You are a young novice monk at Guangxiao Temple, sweeping bodhi leaves every day. Today a stranger from out of town is sitting under the tree, and he will not leave.
guangxiao-bodhi.kidNote: Involves a temple and legend; parental guidance suggested.

guang-1.title: Leaves That Never End
guang-1.text: Before dawn, you sweep bodhi leaves with a bamboo broom. The leaves fall as fast as you sweep them, as if the job can never be finished. A stranger sits under the tree, his clothes soaked through.

guang-2a.title: The Stranger's Question
guang-2a.text: The stranger asks: 'Is this really the tree that was handed down?' You cannot answer. Your teacher said the bodhi tree has withered and grown again, and no one can say for certain what is true.

guang-2b.title: A Leaf on His Shoulder
guang-2b.text: You keep sweeping, and a leaf lands on the stranger's shoulder. He does not brush it off, only closes his eyes. Suddenly you feel that he is not a tourist—he is waiting for something here.

guang-3.title: The Debate of Wind and Banner
guang-3.text: Your teacher points at the banner before the hall: 'Look—is it the wind that moves, or the banner?' Before you can answer, the stranger says: 'It is the mind of a good man that moves.'

guang-4.title: An Old Photograph Under the Tree
guang-4.text: The stranger pulls an old photograph from his bag. In it is his grandfather, standing under this same tree. He says that before his grandfather passed away, he always wanted to come back.

guang-5a.title: A Gust of Wind
guang-5a.text: You sit under the tree, and no one speaks. A breeze blows, and the leaves rustle. The stranger suddenly laughs: 'It sounds like my grandfather coughing here.'

guang-5b.title: The Register in the Guest Hall
guang-5b.text: The guest hall register is full of names, some already faded. The stranger turns to a page and points at a name: 'This is him.' You see a leaf drawn beneath the name.

guang-6.title: Before He Leaves
guang-6.text: The stranger has a bus to catch. Under the tree he picks up a leaf and tucks it into a photo album. You ask whether he will come back next year, and he says: 'Depends on the tree.'

guang-e1.title: Ending · A Look Back at the Temple Gate
guang-e1.text: You walk him to the gate, and the stranger glances back. In that moment you understand: the bodhi tree is not an artifact—it is a thread tying together those who have gone far away.
guang-e1.endingText: The tree has not gone anywhere; it is people who come and go.

guang-e2.title: Ending · New Leaves
guang-e2.text: You go back to sweeping and find new leaves sprouting at the top of the tree. Your teacher says: 'Old leaves fall, new leaves come—that is what keeps a temple alive.' You sweep more slowly, and more quietly.
guang-e2.endingText: What you sweep away is leaves; what you cannot sweep away is remembrance.

guang-2b: Quietly hand him a cup of hot tea

guang-5a: Tell him the tree will grow new leaves again
Quietly sit with him until sunset
guang-5b: Let him look at it himself
guang-6: Walk him to the temple gate

dragonboat-meal.title: The Dragon Boat Feast
dragonboat-meal.subtitle: Pearl River Delta Water Village · One Meal for One Dragon Boat
dragonboat-meal.quote: The dragon boat paddles fast, but the meal is eaten together.
dragonboat-meal.intro: You are a young man on the village dragon boat team. The day before the Dragon Boat Festival, Grandma puts you in charge of the dragon boat feast—dozens of tables are waiting for you to begin.

dragon-1.title: Dozens of Tables
dragon-1.text: Dozens of round tables are set out in front of the ancestral hall. Grandma hands you a list: 'Two hundred catties of pork, a load of choy sum, and enough rice.' You stare at the list, your palms sweating.

dragon-2a.title: Bargaining at the Market
dragon-2a.text: Before dawn, you pedal a tricycle to the market. The pork seller quotes a price twenty percent higher, saying that is simply the festival price. You do not know how to bargain and stand frozen at the stall.

dragon-2b.title: What the Dragon Boat Leader Says
dragon-2b.text: The dragon boat leader is oiling the boat. After hearing you out, he laughs: 'The food does not need to be expensive—what matters most is that it is hot. Go tell the pork seller: this is for the dragon boat team, make it cheaper.'

dragon-3.title: The Feast Begins in the Rain
dragon-3.text: Just as the rice is done, a heavy rain starts. Half the people below the stage leave, and Grandma looks at the sky without a word. You and the other young people hurry to pull out the rain tarps.

dragon-4a.title: The Drum in the Rain
dragon-4a.text: The rain canopy goes up, and the dragon boat drum sounds in the rain. People drift back and sit down, wet as they are. You ladle out the first bowl of rice, your hands still trembling.

dragon-4b.title: Waiting Until Daylight
dragon-4b.text: It rains for two solid hours, and the dishes go cold. People start to leave, and Grandma finally speaks: 'Let us begin—no more waiting.' You hurry to reheat the dishes.

dragon-e1.title: Ending · The First Bowl of Rice
dragon-e1.text: Grandma takes the bowl and puts a piece of pork in it for you first: 'Knowing to serve others first—that is what makes this meal a success.' In the sound of the rain, dozens of tables reach for their chopsticks together.
dragon-e1.endingText: The dragon boat paddles fast, but the meal is eaten together.

dragon-e2.title: Ending · The Last Table
dragon-e2.text: After the dragon boat team finishes eating, you notice one table in the corner untouched. It turns out to belong to the old man who helped carry the drum. You bring him his food, and he grins so wide his eyes nearly disappear.
dragon-e2.endingText: At a meal, what matters most is that no one is left out.

dragon-1: First ask the dragon boat leader
dragon-2a: Pay the price—do not want to hold things up
dragon-2b: Say it just as he taught you

qingming-hill.title: Qingming · Tomb Sweeping
qingming-hill.subtitle: Baiyun Mountain, Guangzhou · A Family's Qingming
qingming-hill.quote: The mountain is still here; generation after generation, the people come.
qingming-hill.intro: On the day of Qingming itself, you carry roast pork and sugarcane up the hill. Dad says that this year you will lead the way.
qingming-hill.kidNote: Involves ancestor rites and parting; parental guidance suggested.

qingming-1.title: The Road Up the Hill
qingming-1.text: The mountain path is wet and slippery, weeds on both sides. Dad walks ahead without a word. You remember that when you were small, Grandpa carried you up here on his back.

qingming-2a.title: Dad Tells an Old Story
qingming-2a.text: Dad suddenly says: 'Grandpa was a carpenter—every door in the village was made by him.' It is the first time you have heard this, and you do not know how to respond.

qingming-2b.title: Mum's Red Paper
qingming-2b.text: Mum takes red paper and a brush from her bag and says she wants to repaint the characters. You look at the faded writing on the stone, and suddenly it feels unfamiliar.

qingming-3.title: Pressing the Paper
qingming-3.text: When you reach the grave, Dad tells you to press the paper. One by one you press the paper money onto the mound; when the wind blows, the corners lift, as if someone is answering.

qingming-4.title: Roast Pork and Sugarcane
qingming-4.text: Mum cuts the roast pork and sets the fattest piece before the stone. Dad peels the sugarcane and, as always, lays the first section down. You ask why, and he says: 'The sweet part is for the ancestors.'

qingming-5a.title: Sweetness in the Palm
qingming-5a.text: You peel it crooked and uneven, and Dad does not laugh—he just takes the knife and demonstrates slowly. Sugarcane juice drips onto your hand, sticky and sweet.

qingming-5b.title: The Writing on the Stone
qingming-5b.text: You crouch down to set out the roast pork and notice a line of small characters carved at the base of the stone—it is Grandpa's name. You reach out and touch it; the stone is cold, yet the characters seem to hold warmth.

qingming-e1.title: Ending · Down the Hill
qingming-e1.text: On the way down, Dad walks slowly. You hold him steady, as Grandpa once held you. The mountain wind rises, paper ash lifts into the air, and slowly settles again.
qingming-e1.endingText: The mountain is still here; generation after generation, the people come.

qingming-e2.title: Ending · Leading the Way Next Year
qingming-e2.text: Dad nods: 'Next year, you lead the way.' You agree, memorising every turn in your heart. So tomb sweeping is not only about sweeping graves—it is about remembering the path.
qingming-e2.endingText: Only when someone remembers the path can someone find their way back.

qingming-1: Walk faster to keep Dad company
Walk slowly and keep an eye on Mum
qingming-2b: Help Mum hold the red paper
Ask whose name is on the stone
qingming-3: Say a few words to the ancestors
qingming-4: Learn to peel sugarcane from Dad
qingming-5a: Ask whether we will come again next year
Tell Dad you have remembered it
qingming-5b: Ask Dad if the paint needs touching up

拜山.meaning: to go up the hill to sweep graves
拜山.note: In Cantonese, visiting graves is called '拜山' (bowing to the mountain).

整.note: In Cantonese, '整' has a very wide range of uses.

示范.note: A written word; in Cantonese one also says '做俾你睇'.
